biographics.title: CTO or VP Engineering at a B2B SaaS / HealthTech / Fintech company
biographics.status: Married, two kids in school, stable
biographics.location: Austin TX, Chicago IL, or remote in a mid-size US city
biographics.education: CS degree, possibly an MBA. Has been coding since college.

psychographics.values: Shipping things that work. Hates rework. Believes technical debt is a compounding tax on every future decision.
psychographics.belief_system: If the architecture is clean, the team ships fast. If it is not, no amount of sprints will fix it.
psychographics.fears: Losing a Series B or strategic acquisition because a technical due diligence revealed a legacy .NET codebase that nobody on their team fully understands anymore.
psychographics.spending_logic: Will pay $80k–$250k for a specialist who can modernize the legacy backend without breaking production — because the alternative is a $2M–$8M valuation haircut or a failed fundraise.

the_crap_he_deals_with: His company is 6–12 years old. The original .NET monolith was written by developers who have long left. His current team works around it, not in it. Every new AI feature the board mandates has to somehow connect to this black box. He has been pitched by three agencies who claimed to understand .NET and Next.js — none of them shipped anything. His board has a 12-month window to demonstrate AI traction or the acquisition conversation dies.
the_hunger: A complete, phased migration plan from the .NET legacy stack to a modern Node.js / Next.js architecture — with zero downtime, real AI integration on the new stack, and a codebase his current team can actually own and extend.

trifecta_alignment.joy: Deep architectural work: strangler-fig migration, domain-driven design, event sourcing on the new stack.
trifecta_alignment.money: A $150k–$300k engagement is less than 5% of the valuation upside from a clean technical due diligence.
trifecta_alignment.mission: Turning a liability into a competitive moat before the board's patience runs out.

cost_of_inaction: Every month the .NET monolith stays in place burns roughly 2–3 sprints of engineering velocity (~$40k in team time fighting legacy issues instead of shipping). At Series B, a legacy backend with no modernization plan costs 20–40% of valuation in a technical due diligence adjustment — on a $10M raise, that is $2M–$4M left on the table. If a competitor modernizes first and ships AI features faster, the acquisition window closes permanently.
trigger_events: Board or investors have formally set a 12-month AI integration deadline — and the legacy stack is the blocker.
A Series B investor has verbally flagged their legacy tech stack as a concern they want resolved before term sheet.
They received preliminary acquisition interest and the buyer's team is going to run technical due diligence in the next 60 days.
A new CTO or VP Eng joined, ran an internal audit, and discovered the debt is larger than anyone knew — too big for the internal team to fix alone.
They tried to hire an agency to modernize the .NET stack and the engagement failed: missed deadlines, broken production, no real progress after 6 months.
hiring_threshold: 1. FINANCIAL PAIN IS DOLLARIZED: They know specifically how much the legacy system is costing them (in valuation suppression, engineering hours, or missed AI revenue). The number is real and large. 2. DEADLINE IS REAL: They have a specific calendar event — a due diligence date, a board review, a fundraising close — that cannot slip. 3. PROOF EXISTS: They need to see that someone has fixed this exact problem (legacy .NET to modern stack) for a company of similar size, with specific outcomes and a timeline.

biographics.title: Founder or Co-Founder of a HealthTech, Fintech, or B2B SaaS company ($2M–$15M ARR)
biographics.status: Divorced or married, 1–2 kids, intensely focused on the company
biographics.location: San Francisco CA, New York NY, Boston MA, or Austin TX
biographics.education: Stanford, MIT, or top-tier university. Technical or business background.
biographics.personal_income: $200k–$350k salary plus $5M–$30M in paper equity at risk

psychographics.values: Speed to exit and maximum valuation. She is done building — she wants to close the deal and move on to the next chapter.
psychographics.belief_system: The product is good enough. The market wants it. The only thing standing between her and a great exit is the technical debt hiding in the codebase from the first three years of building.
psychographics.fears: A buyer's technical due diligence finds the legacy backend — spaghetti code, missing documentation, security gaps, no test coverage — and either kills the deal or cuts $2M–$5M from the offer. Or worse: the deal closes, the acquirer finds the mess post-close, and she faces clawback clauses.
psychographics.spending_logic: Will spend $60k–$150k on a technical cleanup and modernization engagement if it recovers $500k–$3M in acquisition valuation. The math is obvious. She just needs confidence the work will be done right and fast enough.

the_crap_he_deals_with: Her company's codebase has a secret: the first three years were built by a contractor team that no longer exists. The core backend is a mix of outdated Node.js, some .NET remnants, and glue code nobody has touched in years. Her current dev team knows the product but does not fully understand the foundation. An M&A advisor told her last month that technical due diligence is the single most common deal-killer in her valuation range. She has an LOI in draft or an investor who wants to run due diligence in 8 weeks.
the_hunger: A clean, documented, acquisition-ready codebase — with the technical debt identified, quantified, and either remediated or formally documented with a remediation plan. She wants to walk into technical due diligence with confidence, not dread.

trifecta_alignment.joy: Code audit, technical debt triage, targeted refactoring, security hardening, and documentation that a buyer's team can actually understand.
trifecta_alignment.money: VC-funded or profitable, so price is not the issue. Speed and confidence are the issue. A $100k engagement that protects a $5M valuation difference is a trivially easy decision.
trifecta_alignment.mission: Getting to the finish line of a life-defining exit without the technical foundation collapsing in the last 60 days.

cost_of_inaction: Technical debt in a SaaS acquisition suppresses valuation by 20–40% when a buyer's technical due diligence team finds it. On a $10M acquisition, that is $2M–$4M in direct valuation reduction. If the deal collapses entirely — which happens in 30% of SaaS M&A cases due to technical issues — she loses 18–24 months of positioning work and the market window may not reopen. Every week without a clean codebase increases the risk that the next diligence session uncovers something unfixable in the time available.
trigger_events: She has received a Letter of Intent (LOI) from an acquirer and due diligence starts in 30–60 days.
A Series B investor has formally requested a technical audit as a condition of the term sheet.
Her M&A advisor told her that her valuation offer came in 25–40% below her expectation and technical debt was cited as the reason.
A previous acquisition conversation fell apart because technical due diligence revealed issues her team could not explain or defend.
She is 6–12 months from starting a formal sale process and her advisor told her to clean up the codebase first or risk discounting.
hiring_threshold: 1. FINANCIAL PAIN IS DOLLARIZED: She knows the gap between her current valuation and what it should be — and that gap is larger than the cost of fixing it. The number has been said out loud by an advisor or investor. 2. DEADLINE IS REAL: She has a specific date — a due diligence kickoff, a term sheet deadline, or a board-imposed sale timeline — that she cannot push. 3. PROOF EXISTS: She needs to see that someone has prepared a SaaS company of similar size for acquisition technical due diligence and that company closed successfully. Specific industry (HealthTech, Fintech) is a strong bonus.
